extracted.intended_audience: Colonial officials, settlers, missionaries, and Victorian readers interested in Cape York/Port Albany settlement and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th‑century official/report-style travelogue and settlement report describing the geography, climate, natural history, native peoples, and practical recommendations for the Port Albany (Somerset) settlement on Cape York. Written as reports/letters to the Colonial Secretary and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the Somerset settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement should fulfil, 'i.e.', a port of call and harbour of refuge for trade in the dangerous navigation of Torres Straits, and a coal depot for steamers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer explicitly states that the new settlement will 'fulfil admirably the objects for which it was founded'—being a port of call, harbour of refuge, and coal depot (paragraph 29). This is presented as the core measure of the settlement's success, regardless of other local developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural suitability / land evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: No large portion of the land is suited for agriculture; the peculiar climate (dry for eight months of the year) prevents satisfactory cultivation to any large extent; vegetables suitable to the temperature may be grown during the rainy months (December to April).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is based on soil descriptions (reddish sandy loam, ironstone gravel, swampy flats, thin vegetable loam near creeks), extent of sandy/ironstone ground, and seasonal rainfall pattern. Patches near creeks with vegetable loam are identified as suitable for vegetables and bananas (paragraphs 5 and 26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate salubrity as a criterion for settlement desirability
rubrics_metrics.description: The climate is salubrious: no 'local malady', no prevalence of fever or ague, cool nights, regular fresh south‑east breezes, and generally agreeable weather outside the wet season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Haran's medical/meteorological observations are used as evidence (thermometer ranges, absence of sickness during the wet season, hygrometer readings). The absence of noxious exhalations and low incidence of serious illness are highlighted as indicators that Somerset could serve as an accessible sanatorium and is healthy for European residents (paragraphs 27–28 and Dr. Haran's report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Missionary enterprise suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The mainland is likely a barren field for missionary labours because of the unsettled nature of the native people; missionary work might succeed better on neighbouring islands (e.g., Albany, Mount Adolphus) or among islanders (Kororegas, Darnley Islanders) where people are more settled or have higher intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obstacles cited include the natives' unsettled habits (they do not remain in one place), risk beyond protection of the settlement, and differences among groups (Kororegas have higher intelligence through island contact; Banks/Mulgrave Islanders influenced by a resident white man are more cultivated). The writer recommends training young natives on nearby islands following systems used by Bishops Selwyn and Patterson (paragraphs 20–24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of outlying cattle stations
rubrics_metrics.description: A cattle station near the settlement is valuable as an outpost to secure safety, to open up the country, and to provide a ready supply of fresh meat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This judgment is supported by the account of the author's sons establishing a station near Point Vallack, their positive relations with local natives there, and the practical benefits observed (paragraphs 8 and later remarks). The station is also noted as useful in providing an outpost and easing access to surrounding country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for judging an exploration/overland expedition's success
rubrics_metrics.description: An expedition is judged by (a) discoveries of land suitable for pastoral or agricultural occupation, (b) mineral discoveries, and (c) additions to geographical information; failure in (a) and (b) may still be offset by valuable geographic knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overland journey of the Jardine brothers is described as giving a large and valuable addition to geographical information but being 'so far as at present appears, productive of so poor a result' in developing new colony resources (paragraphs 3–5). Practical hardships (loss of supplies, hostile natives, loss of horses, flooded country) are recorded as context for evaluation of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing interactions with native peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful relations and policy must consider natives' mobility, customs, technology (canoe construction, fishing gear), social organization, habits (smoking, food practices), and degrees of contact with islanders/Europeans—these affect their receptiveness to settlement, mission work, and labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report catalogs native dress, shelter, tools and weapons, canoe construction, diet, social customs (corrobories, tattoos/scarification), smoking excesses, and inter-tribal relations; it notes that island contact raises intelligence and that certain tribes are more disposed to work with Europeans (paragraphs 13–19 and 21–24). These observations are offered as practical criteria to shape missionary or colonial policy.
